question: Place the seven steps of the laser printer imaging process in the correct order, beginning with the first step.
explanation: Laser imaging order: Processing (rasterize the page in the formatter), Charging (apply uniform negative charge to the drum), Exposing (laser writes the image by selectively discharging areas), Developing (toner adheres to the discharged areas), Transferring (toner moves from drum to paper), Fusing (heat and pressure bond toner to paper), Cleaning (residual toner is removed from drum).

question: Match each TCP/UDP port number to its associated protocol.
explanation: Core well-known ports for the A+ exam: FTP=21, SSH=22, Telnet=23, SMTP=25, DNS=53, HTTP=80, POP3=110, NetBIOS/NetBT=137-139, IMAP=143, HTTPS=443, SMB/CIFS=445, RDP=3389.

question: Categorize each Ethernet cable category by the highest standard speed it reliably supports at the full 100m run length.
explanation: Cat 5 = 100BASE-TX (100 Mbps). Cat 5e and Cat 6 reliably handle 1 Gbps at 100m — Cat 6 supports 10 Gbps but only up to ~55m. Cat 6a is the lowest category that supports 10GBASE-T at the full 100m. Cat 7 also supports 10 Gbps at 100m. Cat 8 supports up to 40 Gbps but at very short runs (~30m), so its 100m-rated throughput is generally listed as 10 Gbps.

question: Place the six steps of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology in the correct order.
steps: Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory to determine cause
Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
explanation: The CompTIA 6-step troubleshooting methodology must be followed in this order. If testing the theory fails to confirm the cause, you re-establish a new theory (or escalate). Documentation is the final step, not optional — it builds the knowledge base for future incidents.

question: Match each Wi-Fi standard to the frequency band(s) it operates on.
explanation: 802.11a operates in 5 GHz only (~54 Mbps). 802.11b/g are 2.4 GHz only (11/54 Mbps). 802.11n/Wi-Fi 4 is dual-band. 802.11ac/Wi-Fi 5 is 5 GHz only. Wi-Fi 6 (ax) restored dual-band operation. Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6 GHz band on top of Wi-Fi 6's spec.

question: Match each RAID level to its key characteristic.
explanation: RAID 0 stripes data for speed but offers no fault tolerance. RAID 1 mirrors data to two drives — full redundancy but only 50% capacity efficiency. RAID 5 stripes data with distributed parity — survives one drive failure, requires minimum 3 drives. RAID 10 (1+0) mirrors first then stripes the mirrors — combines redundancy and speed, requires minimum 4 drives.

question: Match each cloud service example to its service model.

items.label: AWS Elastic Beanstalk / Azure App Service

explanation: IaaS provides raw VMs/storage/networking — you manage the OS and up. PaaS abstracts the OS — you only manage the app and data. SaaS is finished software delivered over the internet — you only consume it. DaaS delivers a hosted virtual desktop environment streamed to a thin client.

question: Match each connector to the interface it is associated with.
explanation: HDMI and DisplayPort carry video (and audio). RJ45 (twisted pair) and LC (fiber) are network connectors. SATA and M.2 are storage interfaces. 24-pin ATX is the main motherboard power connector; 8-pin EPS supplies the CPU.

question: Place the seven layers of the OSI model in the correct order, starting with Layer 1 at the top.
explanation: OSI layers top-to-bottom (1→7): Physical (cables, signals), Data Link (MAC addresses, switches), Network (IP addresses, routing), Transport (TCP/UDP, port numbers), Session (maintaining connections), Presentation (encryption, compression, format translation), Application (HTTP, FTP, DNS — user-facing protocols). Memory aid: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.'

question: Classify each IPv4 address as private (RFC 1918 — not routable on the public internet) or public.
explanation: RFC 1918 private ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (10.x.x.x), 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16.x.x – 172.31.x.x), and 192.168.0.0/16 (192.168.x.x). Anything outside these three ranges is public. Common traps: 172.32.x.x looks like private but is outside the /12 range; 192.169.x.x looks like private but is above 192.168.

question: Match each USB / interface standard to its maximum theoretical transfer speed.
explanation: USB speed tiers: USB 2.0 = 480 Mbps, USB 3.2 Gen 1 = 5 Gbps, USB 3.2 Gen 2 = 10 Gbps, USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 = 20 Gbps (uses two lanes). USB4 Gen 2x2 = 20 Gbps; USB4 Gen 3x2 = 40 Gbps. Thunderbolt 4 is certified at 40 Gbps minimum. The USB naming scheme was renumbered multiple times — the 'Gen X×Y' format shows speed tier × lane count.

question: Classify each memory or storage type as volatile (loses all data when power is removed) or non-volatile (retains data without power).
explanation: Volatile memory requires constant power to maintain data — DRAM, SRAM, and GDDR are all volatile. Non-volatile storage retains data after power is removed — HDDs, SSDs, ROM chips, and flash drives are all non-volatile. This distinction matters when troubleshooting: a power loss destroys anything in RAM but leaves disk data intact.

question: Match each display symptom to its most likely cause.
categories: Damaged video cable or loose connection

items.label: Screen is very dim — image is barely visible in direct light but present
A tiny fixed dot that stays one color regardless of what is displayed on screen
A faint ghost of a previously displayed UI element is permanently visible on-screen
Display shows distorted or partial image that clears temporarily when the cable is wiggled
items.correct: Damaged video cable or loose connection

explanation: LCD backlight failure leaves the panel dark but functional — shining a flashlight at an angle reveals the image. Dead/stuck pixels are fixed-color dots caused by a transistor failure during manufacturing. Burn-in is permanent pixel degradation from static images on OLED or plasma displays. Cable damage or a loose connector creates intermittent signal artifacts that change when the cable is moved.
